speaker: Hồng Minh
title:
Just five
more minutes.
body:
23:00
A familiar intention.

Have you ever opened a short-video app for five minutes…
and stayed much longer?
notes: Ladies and gentlemen, before we begin, a quick show of hands. How many of you have opened a short-video app intending to watch for just five minutes, only to realise that an hour—or even three—has passed? [Press ‘Let time slip’. Pause for hands.] Thank you. You can put your hands down.

speaker: Hồng Minh
title:
BRAIN
ROT.
body:
Fast. Repetitive. Easy to keep watching.

TikTokInstagram ReelsYouTube Shorts
notes: That experience brings us to brainrot: a term in digital culture associated here with fast, repetitive content offering immediate stimulation. Our study uses a specific survey definition. We are not claiming that every short video is brainrot or that the term is a medical diagnosis.

speaker: Hồng Minh
title:
From internet slang
to Word of the Year.
body:
2024

“brain rot”

Oxford Word of the Year

A cultural signal. A research question.
notes: Oxford selected ‘brain rot’ as its Word of the Year for 2024. That recognition shows the cultural reach of the term; it is not clinical evidence of harm. For our team, it raises a question: what is associated with this viewing pattern among university students?
source: Oxford University Press (2024), cited in the report

speaker: Hồng Minh
title:
What keeps
students scrolling?
body:
An analysis on the determinants of brainrot content consumption among university students in Northern Vietnam

National Economics University · BFT 67A

Triệu Hồng Minh · Trần Ngọc Mai · Lê Cao Thanh
Nguyễn Đức Kiên · Vũ Chí Kiên

Supervisor: Lê Thùy Linh
notes: This is the focus of our research: an analysis of the determinants of brainrot content consumption among university students in Northern Vietnam. We examine platform characteristics alongside social and psychological factors. Our reported results concern associations within the sample.

speaker: Hồng Minh
title: Our research journey.
body:
01

The phenomenon

A familiar viewing loop.

02

The pain point

The user and the platform.

03

The insight

Five potential determinants.

04

The evidence & solution

Results translated into action.
notes: We will follow four stages: the phenomenon, the pain point, the insight, and finally the evidence and solutions. To explore the environment and the motivations behind continued viewing, I will hand over to Mike.

speaker: Mike
title:
A student life.
A continuous feed.
body:
402qualified responses
90.5%studying in Hanoi
69.2%aged 18–20

Classes, assignments and deadlines coexist with
an always-available source of entertainment.
notes: The interesting thing is not simply that we watch. Sometimes we do not realise why we keep watching. We obtained 402 qualified responses, predominantly from students in Hanoi. Around 69 percent were aged 18 to 20. These students face ordinary academic responsibilities while having easy access to short-form content.

speaker: Mike
title:
Within us.
Around us.
body:
Platform-side

The next video
is always ready.

Personalised recommendations
Seamless continuation

User-side

There is a reason
to keep watching.

Peers and trends
Entertainment · Immediate relief
notes: We divide the question into two sides. Platforms personalise recommendations and make continuation effortless. Users also bring social influences, entertainment preferences and a tendency to seek immediate relief. Our dilemma is whether continued viewing is associated with the user, the surrounding environment, or both.

speaker: Mike
title:
The missing
connection.
body:
01

Concept

Brainrot consumption overlaps with—but is not identical to—general short-video use.

02

Explanation

Platform and user factors are often examined in different models.

03

Context

Evidence is still developing for university students in Northern Vietnam.
notes: Our gap concerns the construct, the explanation and the context. We bring five proposed factors into one research framework and apply it to this student sample. The current results examine them separately, so comparing their independent contributions remains a next step. Kiên will now introduce those five factors.

notes: We examine five potential determinants. AI refers to perceived recommendation responsiveness, not artificial intelligence-generated content. UXF concerns effortless continuation. SI captures peer influence; PEV captures enjoyment; PS captures seeking immediate digital relief. Our outcome, BCC, measures unintended and difficult-to-regulate viewing. Each hypothesis proposes a positive association with BCC.
source: Report proposed model and Appendix A

speaker: Nguyễn Đức Kiên
title:

to questions.
body:

Researcher-developed items informed by these concepts; BCC is not the original BRS-14.
notes: The questions were developed from concepts in earlier studies and adapted to our context. For example, recommendation research informs AI, while compensatory internet use informs PS. We are not claiming to reproduce every original scale. Our instrument contains 28 items, including a seven-item BCC measure.

speaker: Nguyễn Đức Kiên
title:
Immediate relief.
Low effort.
body:
3.78/5

Mean PS score

“When I am mentally tired, I am attracted to entertaining content that requires little mental effort.”PS4 · Questionnaire item

An interpretation of survey responses, not evidence that students prefer this over every alternative.
notes: The PS mean is 3.78 out of five. This suggests agreement with statements about seeking accessible, low-effort digital relief. The statement shown is a questionnaire item, not a participant quotation. We cannot conclude that students prefer brainrot over all traditional entertainment. Thành will now explain what the numerical tests actually show.

speaker: Lê Cao Thanh
title:
How we
tested it.
body:
01

Survey

Cross-sectional · Vietnamese questionnaire · 5-point Likert responses.

02

Measurement

28 items across six constructs. Reliability and exploratory structure checks.

03

Relationships

Pearson correlations and five separate simple regressions with BCC.
notes: Our report presents a cross-sectional quantitative survey. We used 28 substantive Likert items across six constructs. We examined descriptions, reliability and exploratory structure before testing relationships. The results shown here are five separate regressions, not one model controlling for all predictors. Optional open responses were supplementary.

Most-used platform over 30 days; viewing duration recalled over 7 days.
notes: TikTok was the most-used platform for 61.7 percent of the sample. Almost half selected the two-to-three-hour or three-plus-hour daily short-video categories. Brainrot-specific exposure was lower: 59.7 percent selected under 15 or 15-to-30 minutes, and 11.4 percent reported none in the past seven days. These are different measures and recall periods; we do not equate all short videos with brainrot.

All five associations are positive and statistically significant. These are correlations, so we cannot conclude that one factor causes consumption or that it has the largest independent effect.

Standardised beta equals Pearson r in these single-predictor models. This is not an adjusted ranking of determinants.

speaker: Lê Cao Thanh
title:
The social context
deserves attention.
body:
Peers and entertainment have the largest observed correlations with BCC in this sample.

A useful direction for action.
Not a causal verdict.
notes: The pattern makes social context and entertainment motives important areas to consider. But platform factors also have positive associations, and we have not isolated independent effects. Our practical question is how to support intentional use while recognising why students watch. Chí Kiên will connect these findings to recommendations.

speaker: Vũ Chí Kiên
title:
For students:
make the stop intentional.
body:
01

Create stopping points

Set a finishing time and use session reminders. UXF r = .357

02

Agree on social boundaries

Shared videos need not receive immediate replies during study. SI r = .673

03

Keep enjoyment planned

Choose entertainment breaks with a clear endpoint. PEV r = .632
notes: Our recommendations combine the original literature and our findings. Qin and colleagues connect system quality with flow, while our UXF result supports considering deliberate stopping points. FOMO literature and our SI result motivate peer agreements around sharing. Entertainment research and our PEV result suggest preserving enjoyment through planned breaks. These are proposals, not interventions we tested.
source: Qin et al. (2022); Przybylski et al. (2013); Zhang et al. (2019) · Report §5.2.1

speaker: Vũ Chí Kiên
title:
For universities:
address the trigger.
body:
Research foundation

Compensatory
internet use

People may seek online relief from unpleasant feelings.

PS ↔ BCC · r = .430
Practical application
  • Recognise boredom and stress-related viewing triggers.
  • Plan alternative short breaks.
  • Build peer-supported study boundaries.
  • Evaluate unplanned viewing and interruptions.
notes: Kardefelt-Winther's compensatory internet use model and Liu and colleagues' stress findings informed PS. Our PS–BCC correlation is .430. Universities could incorporate trigger awareness and break planning into learning-skills activities. Peer involvement can help align boundaries with actual student routines. Evaluate these proposals before scaling them.

speaker: Vũ Chí Kiên
title:
For platforms:
give control a place.
body:
01

Visible time

Session duration and optional reminders.

02

Deliberate continuation

User-selected endpoints and decisions to continue.

03

Understandable recommendations

Clear explanations and accessible content controls.

Design proposals informed by AI (r = .222) and UXF (r = .357); effectiveness requires testing.
notes: Boeker and Urman's audit shows that behaviour shapes recommendations. Combined with our AI result, this motivates clearer explanations and controls. Qin and colleagues' time-distortion findings and our UXF result support testing stopping cues. A successful design should help people stop when intended, rather than assume that more engagement is always better.
source: Boeker & Urman (2022); Qin et al. (2022) · Report §5.2.3

speaker: Vũ Chí Kiên
title:
What we know.
What comes next.
body:
Cross-sectional self-reportLongitudinal studies and viewing diaries
90.5% Hanoi sampleMore institutions and regions
Weaker AI / UXF reliabilityRefine and validate measures in a new sample
Separate regressionsTest predictors together and evaluate interventions
notes: Our study is a snapshot based on self-report and a geographically concentrated sample. AI and UXF reliability also warrants caution. The next steps are broader samples, stronger measurement and simultaneous models. We did not measure clinical addiction, cognitive decline or academic performance as outcomes.

speaker: Research team
title:
Before the next video,
make a choice.
body:
Both the viewing environment and students’ motivations are associated with consumption.

Thank you.Questions & discussion
notes: Our main message is that both platform characteristics and user-side factors are associated with BCC in this sample. Social influence and entertainment show the largest observed correlations. The practical goal is more intentional consumption. Thank you for listening. We welcome your questions.
